body.heading: A month-long spending spree that left a paper trail
paragraphs: Court filings paint a picture of extravagant spending in the weeks after the theft in August 2024. Prosecutors say Lam and his co-defendants bought fleets of sports cars, chartered private jets, hired personal security and rented luxury mansions in Miami and the Hamptons. The group is said to have spent roughly $4 million at Los Angeles nightclubs over about a month, with Lam alone allegedly spending more than $569,000 during a single night out.

That spending trail proved central to how investigators built the case. Lam, described in reporting as an eighth-grade dropout, was arrested at a Miami mansion on September 18, 2024, the same day a co-defendant, Jean Erick Serrano, was taken into custody at Los Angeles International Airport wearing a watch valued at roughly $500,000.

body.heading: A network unraveling one plea at a time
paragraphs: Other defendants in the case have already faced sentencing. Tucker Desmond, who pleaded guilty to destroying evidence tied to other plotters' crimes, was sentenced to probation after apologizing at his hearing in March for what he described as chasing an image of success rather than genuine achievement. A co-defendant named Ferro declined to speak at his own sentencing in May, where the judge rejected an attorney's characterization of the group as mischievous young men, noting that age only explains so much.

The case has drawn attention within the cryptocurrency industry as a stark illustration of how social-engineering attacks, rather than technical hacking, remain one of the most effective ways criminals target crypto holders. Investigators say the pattern, gaining trust by impersonating a trusted platform, then moving quickly to drain and launder funds, has become increasingly common as digital asset holdings have grown large enough to make individual victims worth targeting directly.

Prosecutors have framed the case as part of a broader crackdown on organized crypto-theft rings that emerged in the early 2020s, many of them built around young defendants who met online before coordinating real-world heists. With ten defendants having already pleaded guilty and Lam's plea expected to make eleven, legal observers say the remaining defendants in the eighteen-person case are likely to face mounting pressure to negotiate similar deals rather than risk trial, given how much of the underlying evidence, including the spending records, has already been laid out in court filings.

articles.title: SEC Sues Proxy Giant ISS Over Withheld Voting Data
articles.dek: The SEC is suing Institutional Shareholder Services to force it to hand over years of client voting records, as scrutiny of proxy advisers intensifies.
articles.author: daniel-cho
articles.imageAlt: A courthouse building facade with tall stone columns
takeaways: The SEC filed suit on September 4 to force ISS, which advises institutional investors on more than 90% of proxy votes alongside rival Glass Lewis, to comply with a subpoena.
The agency wants four years of client-identifying voting records; ISS says handing them over raises First Amendment and retaliation concerns.
The case follows a December executive order directing the SEC to tighten oversight of proxy advisers, part of a broader push that also includes a Justice Department antitrust review.

body.heading: A subpoena fight reaches federal court
paragraphs: The Securities and Exchange Commission filed a subpoena-enforcement action on September 4 in the US District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania, seeking to compel Institutional Shareholder Services, known as ISS, to comply with an outstanding request for records. The SEC, which regulates ISS as a registered investment adviser, says the firm has refused to turn over information central to how it makes its proxy voting recommendations.

According to the SEC's filing, its Division of Examinations opened a routine review of ISS in March, requesting data related to the firm's proxy recommendations and voting activity so it could evaluate ISS's compliance with federal securities law. When ISS did not fully comply, the agency escalated the matter, issuing a formal administrative subpoena on July 21 that the company has also only partly answered.

body.heading: Four years of client voting records at stake
paragraphs: The records the SEC is demanding cover roughly four years of client-identifying proxy voting data, a level of detail ISS has resisted providing. The agency has been explicit that the case is narrowly about compelling compliance with an information request, not an allegation that ISS violated securities laws; the underlying examination has not reached any conclusion about wrongdoing.

ISS has pushed back on First Amendment grounds, arguing in correspondence with the agency that disclosing detailed information about its recommendations and its clients' voting activity could expose both the firm and its clients to retaliation. The company agreed to two of the SEC's three information requests but refused the third, which covers the voting database at the core of its business.

body.heading: Part of a broader push against proxy advisers
paragraphs: The lawsuit lands amid a wider Trump administration effort to rein in the influence of proxy advisory firms. A December executive order directed the SEC to review its rules on proxy advisers, enforce antifraud provisions more aggressively, and consider new disclosure requirements, specifically naming ISS and Glass Lewis as controlling more than 90% of the US proxy-advisory market.

The pressure campaign extends beyond the SEC. The Justice Department announced in August that it plans to rescind a 1987 approval letter that had shielded ISS's proxy recommendations from antitrust scrutiny, citing concerns about market concentration. Separately, the Department of Labor issued guidance in April establishing that proxy advisory firms can be treated as fiduciaries under federal pension law when they issue voting recommendations, a designation that could expose them to new legal liability.

body.heading: Why the outcome could ripple through corporate boardrooms
paragraphs: ISS and Glass Lewis wield outsized influence over how large institutional investors, including pension funds and mutual funds, vote on matters ranging from board elections to executive pay packages and shareholder proposals. Because so many investors follow their recommendations closely, a shift in how those firms operate, or in how transparent they are forced to be about their methodology, could meaningfully change the balance of power between company management and shareholders at annual meetings.

ISS is not new to regulatory scrutiny: the firm settled with the SEC in 2013, paying a $300,000 penalty over allegations it improperly shared confidential client information. Founded in 1985 and acquired by Deutsche Börse, the operator of the Frankfurt Stock Exchange, in 2020 for 1.5 billion euros, ISS's foreign ownership has itself become a point of criticism in the current political debate, with the White House highlighting it as a factor in its push for tighter oversight.

For now, the court's role is narrowly defined: a judge in Philadelphia will decide only whether the SEC's subpoena is properly authorized, relevant to a legitimate inquiry and not unreasonably burdensome, a standard that appeals courts in the region have historically described as very difficult for a company resisting a subpoena to overcome. Whatever the outcome, the case is widely seen as a preview of further fights to come, given that Glass Lewis, ISS's main rival, faces many of the same political and regulatory pressures and has yet to be tested in court.

articles.title: China Extends Gold-Buying Streak to 22 Months Running
articles.dek: China's central bank kept adding to its gold reserves in August, its 22nd straight monthly increase, as bullion holds near record highs on rate jitters.
articles.author: priya-menon
articles.imageAlt: Stacks of gold bars arranged closely together
takeaways: China's central bank extended its gold-buying streak to a 22nd consecutive month in August, lifting official holdings to 76.73 million fine troy ounces.
Gold has pulled back to around $4,400 an ounce after a volatile year, still up more than 21% from a year earlier despite recent losses.
The steady official buying comes as bond yields worldwide climb and central banks diversify away from a heavier reliance on the dollar.

body.heading: Beijing keeps buying, month after month
paragraphs: China's central bank added to its official gold reserves for a 22nd consecutive month in August, according to data released this week, extending one of the longest sustained buying streaks in the People's Bank of China's history. The purchases lifted the bank's holdings to 76.73 million fine troy ounces, continuing a steady accumulation that has persisted through sharp swings in gold's price over the past year.

The consistency of the buying stands out against a backdrop of significant volatility in the broader gold market. Prices touched a record above $5,000 an ounce earlier in the year before falling by as much as 18% from that peak, then staged a sharp rebound, before pulling back again more recently toward the $4,400 level amid renewed expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike.

body.heading: A broader trend among global central banks
paragraphs: China is far from alone in steadily building gold reserves. Central banks around the world have been adding to their gold holdings for several years as part of a broader effort to diversify foreign exchange reserves away from a heavy reliance on the US dollar, a trend that has accelerated amid periodic bouts of dollar volatility and rising geopolitical tension. Gold offers central banks an asset with no counterparty risk, meaning it cannot be frozen or sanctioned the way foreign currency reserves held in another country's banking system can be.

That dynamic has taken on additional significance this year given the scale of currency intervention some governments have had to undertake. Japan, for instance, has spent a record amount defending the yen in recent months, drawing down its own foreign reserves in the process, a reminder of how exposed reserve portfolios can be when they are concentrated in a single currency or asset class.

body.heading: Gold's rocky path through 2026
paragraphs: Gold's price action this year illustrates just how divided investor sentiment toward the metal has become. After setting fresh records early in 2026, bullion fell to a session low near $4,376 an ounce earlier this month following a stronger-than-expected US jobs report, before recovering part of that loss. As of this week, gold was trading around $4,400 an ounce, essentially flat over the past month but still up roughly 21% compared with the same time last year.

Short-term traders have been reacting sharply to shifting expectations for Fed policy, since gold pays no yield and becomes relatively less attractive when interest rates rise. Central bank buyers like China's, by contrast, appear to be operating on a much longer time horizon, treating monthly price swings as largely irrelevant to a strategy focused on gradually building a larger, more diversified reserve base over years rather than weeks.

body.heading: What could shift the picture next
paragraphs: Analysts will be watching upcoming US inflation data and the Federal Reserve's mid-September meeting closely, since another signal of a possible rate hike could pressure gold prices further in the near term, even as central bank demand provides a longer-term floor. Any escalation in the ongoing Middle East conflict between the US and Iran could also cut the other way, reviving safe-haven buying that has periodically supported gold even during periods of rising rates.

For now, China's steady accumulation offers a useful contrast to the volatility playing out in daily trading. While retail and institutional investors have been whipsawed by shifting rate expectations, official buyers appear to be treating gold less as a short-term trade and more as a structural hedge against currency and geopolitical risk, a distinction that market watchers say helps explain why the metal has managed to hold well above where it traded just a few years ago, even after its recent pullback.

Some analysts also point out that China's buying pattern rarely moves in lockstep with headline price swings, since the People's Bank of China tends to disclose its reserve changes with a lag and in relatively modest monthly increments rather than large, market-moving purchases. That approach appears deliberate: a central bank absorbing gold gradually over nearly two years avoids drawing the kind of attention that a sudden, large purchase might invite, while still steadily building a reserve cushion that reduces its dependence on any single foreign currency over the medium to long term.

articles.title: 'Spider-Man' Powers Summer to All-Time Box Office High
articles.dek: Sony's 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' held No. 1 for a sixth straight weekend, helping push US summer ticket sales to a record near $4.76 billion.
articles.author: marcus-obi
articles.imageAlt: Rows of empty red cinema seats facing a large screen
takeaways: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' spent a sixth consecutive weekend at No. 1, crossing $900 million domestically faster than any film in history.
US summer ticket sales reached roughly $4.76 billion, edging past the previous record of $4.755 billion set in 2013.
The record came despite several high-profile flops, including Disney's live-action 'Moana' and Warner Bros.' 'Supergirl.'

body.heading: A record summer, decided on the final weekend
paragraphs: Hollywood's summer box office finished in a photo finish, with domestic ticket sales landing at roughly $4.76 billion between May and early September, according to data from Rentrak. That figure edges out the prior all-time high of $4.755 billion set back in 2013, making 2026 the biggest summer moviegoing season on record, unadjusted for inflation.

The season came down to the wire over Labor Day weekend, when studios and box office analysts were still uncertain whether the final tally would clear the 2013 mark. Rentrak had flagged a chance the summer could finish anywhere from $8 million below the record to several million above it, depending on how the four-day holiday weekend played out.

body.heading: 'Spider-Man' just keeps climbing
paragraphs: Sony and Marvel's 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' did most of the heavy lifting. The film held the No. 1 spot at the domestic box office for a sixth consecutive weekend, a rare feat that reflects both its staying power and a relatively thin slate of new competition. It earned about $18 million over the traditional three-day weekend and was projected to bring in roughly $23.3 million through the Labor Day holiday.

The film's records go well beyond weekly rankings. It became only the second movie in history, after 2015's 'Star Wars: The Force Awakens,' to cross $900 million domestically, and it did so in just 36 days, compared with 50 days for 'Force Awakens.' It also set the record for the biggest single Tuesday in domestic box office history, taking in $42 million, and became the highest-grossing film of the year worldwide with more than $1.1 billion, edging past Disney and Pixar's 'Toy Story 5.'

body.heading: A season built on hits, not just one franchise
paragraphs: 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' wasn't carrying the summer alone. Other studio releases including 'The Odyssey,' 'Toy Story 5' and 'The Devil Wears Prada 2' turned in strong performances, while indie sleeper hits like 'Obsession' and 'Backrooms' added unexpected upside outside the usual blockbuster mix. August alone brought in an all-time record $1.276 billion domestically, unseating a mark set back in August 2016.

Not every big-budget bet paid off. Disney's live-action 'Moana,' Warner Bros. and DC's 'Supergirl,' and Amazon MGM's 'Masters of the Universe' all underperformed expectations, underscoring how uneven the summer was beneath its record-setting headline number. Universal ultimately led all studios for the season with $1.23 billion in domestic revenue.

body.heading: A sign of a genuine industry rebound, or a one-off?
paragraphs: For an industry still recovering from pandemic-era disruptions and a prolonged 2023 labor strike, the summer's numbers offer some of the clearest evidence yet that audiences are willing to return to theaters in force when the right films are on offer. Industry analysts have pointed to the sheer number of billion-dollar global hits this year as a particularly encouraging sign, since no year since 2019 had produced more than three films crossing that threshold before 2026.

Whether that momentum carries into the fall remains to be seen. Hollywood has several more high-profile releases queued up in the coming months, and executives are hoping the year's total domestic haul can approach $10 billion, a figure that regularly came within reach before the pandemic but has proven elusive since. For now, exhibitors are treating the record summer as validation that a well-marketed blockbuster can still reliably fill theater seats.

articles.title: Jane Fonda Slams Paramount-Warner Merger at Venice Gala
articles.dek: At the DVF Awards in Venice, Jane Fonda called the pending Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger 'terrible' for consumers, workers and creatives.
articles.author: priya-menon
articles.imageAlt: A grand red-carpet event with elegant lighting and a formal gathering
takeaways: Jane Fonda, honored at the 17th DVF Awards in Venice, renewed her opposition to Paramount Skydance's roughly $111 billion bid for Warner Bros. Discovery.
She argued the deal would raise consumer prices, cost thousands of jobs and weaken bargaining power for creatives and unions.
Fonda separately defended actor Mark Ruffalo, alleging a modern industry blacklist after he was accused of antisemitism for criticizing the merger.

body.heading: A pointed message at a glamorous gala
paragraphs: Jane Fonda used her platform at the DVF Awards charity gala in Venice on Thursday to renew her public opposition to the proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery by Paramount Skydance, a deal reportedly valued at around $111 billion. Speaking to a small group of journalists before being honored at the ceremony, the 88-year-old actress and longtime activist laid out a detailed case against the merger.

Fonda argued that the heavy debt load carried by the Ellison family, which controls Paramount Skydance, made the deal financially fragile even as it moved forward. She said the merger would raise prices for consumers, cost thousands of industry jobs, and leave creatives with fewer studios to pitch their work to, weakening bargaining power for both individual talent and entertainment unions.

body.heading: Opposing the deal while praising its architect
paragraphs: Notably, Fonda's criticism of the merger came paired with warm personal comments about Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison, whom she said she likes very much. She noted that Ellison's Skydance banner had financed her Netflix series 'Grace and Frankie,' which ended its run in 2022, and made clear that her fondness for him personally did not soften her professional concerns about the deal.

Fonda also invoked her former partner, media mogul Ted Turner, arguing he would be heartbroken to see Paramount potentially gain control of CNN, a network he once built and was famously reluctant to part with. She framed the merger not as a routine business transaction but as a structural threat to the broader media landscape.

body.heading: Defending Mark Ruffalo and alleging a blacklist
paragraphs: Fonda's remarks extended beyond the merger's financial terms into allegations of retaliation against critics of the deal. She said actor Mark Ruffalo, who had previously spoken out against the merger and drawn connections between Larry Ellison's Oracle and the Israeli military, was subsequently accused by Larry Ellison of antisemitism, a charge Fonda characterized as a deliberate tactic to silence dissent.

Asked directly whether a modern-day industry blacklist was operating against critics of the deal, Fonda answered without hesitation that it was, describing it as a tactic being actively used against those who speak up. She said she remained undeterred by political pressure more broadly, including from President Trump, stating flatly that he could do nothing to intimidate her.

body.heading: A star-studded evening with a wider message
paragraphs: The 17th annual DVF Awards, organized by fashion designer Diane von Furstenberg to honor extraordinary women, also recognized Barbados Prime Minister Mia Amor Mottley, Pulitzer Prize-winning photojournalist Lynsey Addario, Food4Education founder Wawira Njiru, and French feminist figure Gisèle Pelicot. The event drew a crowd that included Barry Diller, Fareed Zakaria and California's Jennifer Siebel Newsom, among other prominent guests.

Fonda's comments landed at a moment when the Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger already faces resistance on multiple fronts, adding another high-profile voice to a debate that has increasingly pitted industry veterans against consolidating media conglomerates. With David Ellison reportedly working on written commitments meant to ease concerns about the deal's impact, Fonda's remarks suggest that skepticism from Hollywood's old guard is unlikely to fade quietly.

articles.title: 'The Pitt' Leads Emmy Field Ahead of Sunday's Ceremony
articles.dek: HBO Max's medical drama 'The Pitt' topped this year's Emmy nominations with 25, as the 78th Primetime Emmys near their September 14 broadcast.
articles.author: hana-fujimoto
articles.imageAlt: A television studio soundstage with bright overhead lighting rigs
takeaways: 'The Pitt' leads all shows with 25 Emmy nominations, followed by 'Hacks' with 24, a record for a single comedy season.
Mariska Hargitay hosts the 78th Primetime Emmy Awards on September 14, shifted to a Monday broadcast because of an NFL game on NBC.
The Creative Arts Emmys were handed out September 5 and 6, setting the stage for the main ceremony at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles.

body.heading: A medical drama tops the field
paragraphs: HBO Max's emergency-room drama 'The Pitt' enters this year's Primetime Emmy Awards as the most-nominated show, having picked up 25 nominations across acting, writing and technical categories. The show, which won Outstanding Drama Series at last year's ceremony, built its haul in part on a deep bench of nominated cast members playing doctors and staff at its fictional Pittsburgh hospital.

Close behind is 'Hacks,' also from HBO Max, which earned 24 nominations for its final season, a record for a single season of a comedy series. The strong showing from both shows helped HBO Max lead all platforms with 122 total nominations, ahead of rivals including Apple TV, which had a breakout year of its own with new series 'Pluribus,' 'Margo's Got Money Troubles' and 'Widow's Bay' all earning multiple nods.

body.heading: A Monday night ceremony, for the first time in years
paragraphs: The 78th Primetime Emmy Awards will air live on NBC on Monday, September 14, at 8 p.m. ET from the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles, shifting from the traditional Sunday slot because of a scheduled NFL game on the network. 'Law & Order: Special Victims Unit' star Mariska Hargitay, who begins her 28th season on that long-running series this fall, will host the broadcast.

Ahead of the main event, the Creative Arts Emmys, which recognize technical and craft achievements, were handed out over two nights on September 5 and 6 at the Television Academy. Those ceremonies typically award categories such as production design, cinematography and stunt coordination, and their results often foreshadow which shows are best positioned heading into the main telecast.

body.heading: A crowded drama and comedy race
paragraphs: This year's Outstanding Drama Series category includes 'The Diplomat,' 'The Gilded Age,' 'A Knight of the Seven Kingdoms,' 'Paradise,' 'The Pitt,' 'Pluribus,' 'Slow Horses' and 'Your Friends & Neighbours,' a lineup that mixes established prestige dramas with several first-time nominees. On the comedy side, 'Abbott Elementary,' 'The Bear,' 'Hacks,' 'Margo's Got Money Troubles,' 'Nobody Wants This,' 'Only Murders in the Building,' 'Shrinking' and 'Widow's Bay' round out the field.

The acting races feature a similarly wide mix of veterans and newcomers. Supporting categories on the drama side include multiple nominees from 'The Pitt' itself, reflecting the show's ensemble strength, while lead acting categories include Yahya Abdul-Mateen II for 'Wonder Man,' Steve Carell for 'Rooster' and Quinta Brunson for 'Abbott Elementary,' among others.

body.heading: What's at stake heading into Monday
paragraphs: With 'The Pitt' returning as the defending Outstanding Drama Series winner and now the most-nominated show overall, the ceremony will test whether the show can convert its nomination lead into a repeat win against a deep field of competitors, several of them first-time Emmy contenders. 'Hacks,' meanwhile, closes out its run with its strongest nomination total yet, giving the comedy a chance to cement its legacy in its final eligible season.

Beyond the marquee races, this year's Emmys will also be watched for how streaming platforms continue to reshape the television landscape, with Apple TV's strong showing suggesting the field of contenders for top honors is growing more crowded and less predictable than in recent years. Industry watchers say the results could offer an early signal of which platforms and genres are best positioned heading into next year's awards cycle.

articles.title: NASA's Roman Telescope Launches on Dark Universe Hunt
articles.dek: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched aboard a Falcon Heavy rocket, beginning a three-month journey to study dark matter, dark energy and exoplanets.
articles.author: sofia-reyes
articles.imageAlt: A rocket launch lighting up the night sky with a bright exhaust trail
takeaways: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched August 30 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy, beginning a three-month, million-mile journey to its L2 orbit.
Roman shares Hubble's mirror size but surveys 100 times more sky per snapshot, and is designed to work roughly a thousand times faster.
The telescope will send back 1.4 terabytes of data daily, the highest rate of any NASA astrophysics mission, with first images expected by early 2027.

body.heading: A tour-bus-sized telescope leaves Earth
paragraphs: NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope lifted off at 7:26 a.m. EDT on August 30 aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket from Launch Complex 39A at Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The roughly 18,000-pound observatory, about the size of a tour bus, separated from the rocket's upper stage 31 minutes after launch and began the first steps of a three-month, million-mile journey to its final orbital position.

Roman is headed to the second Sun-Earth Lagrange point, known as L2, located about a million miles from Earth in the direction opposite the sun. Unlike Hubble, which orbits Earth, Roman will orbit the sun directly, following the same general strategy NASA used for the James Webb Space Telescope.

body.heading: Same mirror as Hubble, a much wider view
paragraphs: Roman's primary mirror is the same size as Hubble's, but the telescope is built to capture roughly 100 times more sky in a single snapshot. That leap comes from a more curved primary mirror, a secondary mirror positioned closer to the primary, and a considerably larger main camera, a combination that lets Roman survey vast swaths of the cosmos far more quickly than its predecessor.

NASA says the telescope is designed to survey the universe about a thousand times faster than Hubble. That capability is expected to support the discovery of far more supernovas, which help scientists understand the universe's expansion rate and composition, along with a broad new census of planets orbiting other stars.

body.heading: Chasing dark matter, dark energy and distant worlds
paragraphs: The mission's central goals are to investigate dark energy and dark matter, two of the most persistent mysteries in modern physics, while also conducting a statistical census of planetary systems beyond our own. Roman is expected to enable a wide range of additional astrophysics research well beyond those core objectives, given the sheer volume of sky it will be able to observe.

The telescope will generate about 1.4 terabytes of data every day, the highest data rate of any NASA astrophysics mission to date. Given that volume, NASA plans to lean on machine learning, artificial intelligence and citizen scientists to help sift through the incoming data and flag potentially significant findings for astronomers to study in more detail.

body.heading: Months of setup before the first images
paragraphs: Roman now enters a commissioning period that NASA expects to last several weeks, during which engineers will deploy its solar panels, perform a mid-course correction burn, and run its instruments through a series of calibrations and tests to confirm everything is functioning as designed. NASA anticipates releasing Roman's first science images by early 2027.

The mission is managed by NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, with participation from the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Caltech/IPAC and the Space Telescope Science Institute, alongside a broader science team drawn from research institutions around the country. The telescope is named after Nancy Grace Roman, NASA's first chief of astronomy, who helped lay the groundwork for the agency's space telescope program decades before Roman itself took shape.

articles.title: Hubble Finds a Mysterious 10-Sided Wave on Saturn
articles.dek: Astronomers confirmed a giant decagon-shaped atmospheric wave circling Saturn's south pole, a striking counterpart to its famous northern hexagon.
articles.author: daniel-cho
articles.imageAlt: The planet Saturn and its rings set against the darkness of space
takeaways: An international team confirmed a 10-sided atmospheric wave, or decagon, circling Saturn's south pole, published September 2 in Science Advances.
Unlike the planet's famous northern hexagon, which has held steady for more than 40 years, the decagon appears to be a newer feature that is still strengthening.
Researchers traced faint hints of the pattern back to 2023 Hubble images, but believe it likely formed sometime between 2017 and 2023, when the pole was hidden from view.

body.heading: A southern counterpart to Saturn's famous hexagon
paragraphs: An international team of astronomers led by Agustín Sánchez-Lavega of the University of the Basque Country has confirmed the existence of a giant, 10-sided atmospheric wave encircling Saturn's south pole, a striking new companion to the planet's long-known northern hexagon. The findings were published September 2 in the journal Science Advances, based on observations gathered through NASA's Hubble Space Telescope.

Saturn's north pole has been ringed by a stable, six-sided cloud pattern since it was first spotted in Voyager spacecraft data in 1987, and the northern hexagon has remained a consistent feature every time scientists have observed it in the decades since. The newly confirmed southern decagon appears to be something different: a feature that is actively strengthening rather than sitting in a long-term stable state.

body.heading: Piecing together years of scattered observations
paragraphs: Researchers traced faint early hints of the decagon back to Hubble images from 2023, gathered as part of the telescope's Outer Planet Atmospheres Legacy program, which has photographed the outer planets annually for more than a decade. Ground-based amateur and professional astronomers noted an undulating band around the pole in 2024, and the pattern sharpened into a clearly defined 10-sided shape in Hubble images taken in 2025.

Pinning down exactly when the decagon first formed has proven difficult. Saturn's axial tilt means the planet experiences seasons much like Earth does, and its south pole was turned away from Earth's view between 2012 and 2023, along with the fact that no orbiting spacecraft has studied the planet up close since NASA's Cassini mission ended in 2017. As a result, scientists believe the feature likely emerged sometime in that six-year window when direct observation wasn't possible.

body.heading: A wave embedded deep in the atmosphere
paragraphs: Scientists describe the decagon as a large atmospheric wave embedded within one of Saturn's powerful jet streams, likely formed where fast-moving gas farther from the pole interacts with slower-moving gas closer to it. Observations show the wave extends through multiple layers of Saturn's atmosphere, indicating it is a substantial three-dimensional weather system rather than a shallow, cloud-level pattern.

Amy Simon, a co-author of the study and principal investigator of the OPAL program at NASA's Goddard Space Flight Center, said the team had never seen anything quite like this feature in Saturn's southern hemisphere, noting the contrast with the northern hexagon's four-decade stability. The scale of the discovery is difficult to overstate: the decagon wraps around the entire polar region of a planet more than nine times wider than Earth.

body.heading: Watching a weather system evolve in real time
paragraphs: The research team presented its findings at the Europlanet Science Congress on September 7, putting the discovery in front of the broader planetary science community for further scrutiny. Hubble is scheduled to observe Saturn again later this month, which should help researchers determine whether the decagon's sharpening trend has continued or begun to level off.

Scientists also plan to enlist the James Webb Space Telescope, which can observe Saturn's atmosphere in infrared wavelengths beyond Hubble's optical reach, to probe the decagon's vertical structure, temperature profile and composition. Computer modeling is planned as well, to test candidate explanations for how the wave formed, including the possibility that a nearby storm perturbed the jet stream into its current geometric shape. Researchers say the coming months of observation should help clarify whether the decagon is a fleeting feature or one capable of persisting for decades, the way its northern counterpart has.

articles.title: NASA Delays Crew-13 Launch After Dragon Fuel Leak
articles.dek: NASA and SpaceX postponed the Crew-13 mission to the ISS after finding an oxidizer leak in Dragon's propulsion system, pushing liftoff into late September.
articles.author: hana-fujimoto
articles.imageAlt: A crewed space capsule mounted atop a rocket on the launch pad
takeaways: NASA and SpaceX postponed Crew-13's September 12 launch to the ISS after finding an oxidizer leak in the Dragon capsule's propulsion system.
The four-person crew includes NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney, Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk and Roscosmos's Sergey Teteryatnikov.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said repairs could take two to four weeks, pushing the earliest realistic launch window to late September or early October.

body.heading: A leak found during routine prelaunch checks
paragraphs: NASA and SpaceX announced on August 29 that they were postponing the launch of the Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station after engineers discovered an oxidizer leak in the propulsion system of the mission's Dragon spacecraft. The issue turned up during standard prelaunch processing at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, ahead of what had been a planned September 12 liftoff.

The Canadian Space Agency, whose astronaut Joshua Kutryk is part of the four-person crew, was among the first to confirm the delay publicly, posting that an oxidizer leak had been discovered on Dragon's propulsion system. Joint NASA and SpaceX teams began conducting additional testing and reviewing data to determine what repairs would be needed before the capsule could fly.

body.heading: A four-person, multinational crew waits it out
paragraphs: Crew-13 is set to carry NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins, serving as commander, and Luke Delaney as pilot, alongside Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk and Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov as mission specialists. Once aboard the station, the crew will join Expedition 75, continuing the steady rotation of long-duration missions that has kept the ISS staffed for more than two decades.

The mission marks the 13th operational crew rotation under NASA's Commercial Crew Program and the 21st crewed orbital flight for a Dragon spacecraft overall, underscoring how routine, if not risk-free, these launches have become. The flight is also notable for a change in ground operations, with SpaceX replacing its traditional armored emergency-egress vehicles at the launch pad with customized Tesla Cybertrucks.

body.heading: What exactly went wrong
paragraphs: The leak involves nitrogen tetroxide, the oxidizer half of the hypergolic propellant that powers Dragon's 18 Draco thrusters, each capable of producing 400 newtons of thrust. Those thrusters rely on nitrogen tetroxide paired with monomethylhydrazine as fuel; the two chemicals ignite spontaneously on contact, a property that lets Dragon maneuver in orbit and dock with the space station without a separate ignition system.

NASA has not disclosed precisely where in the propulsion system the leak occurred or named the specific Dragon capsule involved, and the agency has not announced a fleetwide inspection of other Dragon spacecraft as a result. Isolating the source of a leak in a hypergolic propulsion system typically requires careful diagnostic work, since the chemicals involved are highly reactive and toxic, demanding methodical testing rather than a quick fix.

body.heading: A two- to four-week wait, at minimum
paragraphs: Speaking a day after the delay was announced, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said the repair work could take two to four weeks, a timeline that pushes the earliest realistic launch window toward late September or early October. Isaacman made the comments while attending the launch of NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, which lifted off successfully the following day despite the unrelated Dragon issue grounding Crew-13.

In the meantime, the four astronauts, who were already partway through the standard two-week quarantine protocol ahead of a crewed launch, will need to adjust their preparations around the new timeline. NASA says it will announce a firm new launch date once the leak has been fully diagnosed, repaired if necessary, and retested under realistic prelaunch conditions.
